subject: Critical Thinking
title: Heuristics: Mental Shortcuts with a Price
description: A 60-second lesson on Heuristics: Mental Shortcuts with a Price.

hook.text: A heuristic is a rule of thumb: 'If it looks like a duck and quacks like a duck...' Usually right. Sometimes lethal.

buildup.text: Heuristics let us decide fast with limited information. Without them, ordering lunch would take an hour.

discovery.text: Kahneman identified three key heuristics: availability, representativeness, and anchoring. Each creates specific biases.

twist.text: The same shortcut that saves you time at the grocery store can lose you millions in the stock market.

climax.text: Heuristics aren't errors — they're trade-offs between speed and accuracy. The key is knowing when accuracy matters.

punchline.text: Shortcuts work — until the stakes are high.

quiz.question: What are heuristics?
options: Mental shortcuts that trade accuracy for speed

details.summary: Heuristics are cognitive shortcuts that let you make fast decisions with limited information. They often work well but can lead to systematic errors when applied in the wrong context.
details.whyItMatters: Every quick judgment you make relies on heuristics. Understanding them helps you know when to trust your gut and when to slow down.
takeaways: They work well in familiar, time-pressured situations

faq.question: What is a common example of a heuristic used every day?
faq.answer: The recognition heuristic: if you recognize one brand but not another, you assume the recognized one is better. This shortcut works often enough that we rely on it without thinking, but it can lead us astray.

faq.question: How do heuristics relate to cognitive biases?
faq.answer: Heuristics are the mental shortcuts; biases are the systematic errors those shortcuts produce. Every cognitive bias can be traced back to a heuristic that works in some contexts but fails in others.
